# 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise: Public Evidence Chain

## Executive assessment

The strongest publicly documented evidence indicates that the 2023 3CX compromise began not with a direct initial intrusion into 3CX, but through an earlier compromise of Trading Technologies software and infrastructure. Mandiant identified a maliciously modified X_TRADER installer, distributed from the legitimate Trading Technologies website, as the initial compromise vector into the 3CX network. The installer deployed the VEILEDSIGNAL backdoor. Mandiant characterized this as one software supply-chain compromise leading to another. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

After entering the 3CX environment, the threat actor harvested credentials, moved laterally, and compromised both Windows and macOS build environments. Mandiant identified malware and persistence mechanisms on those build systems, including TAXHAUL and COLDCAT on Windows and POOLRAT on macOS. The available evidence establishes compromise of the build environment, but does not disclose the exact build-pipeline modification, account used, or precise mechanism by which malicious code was inserted into each release. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The compromised build and release process produced trojanized 3CX DesktopApp packages. Mandiant identified affected versions as 18.12.416 and earlier. The malicious application executed SUDDENICON, which retrieved command-and-control information from encrypted icons hosted on GitHub and downloaded ICONICSTEALER, an information-stealing payload. Kaspersky separately described infected MSI and macOS installers, a malicious DLL, shellcode embedded in the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`, and subsequent deployment of an infostealer and, in some cases, the Gopuram backdoor. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

Attribution remains qualified rather than conclusive. Mandiant assessed the activity as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and assessed with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. CrowdStrike associated the attack with Labyrinth Chollima. Kaspersky connected Gopuram to earlier AppleJeus activity and noted that AppleJeus had been attributed to Lazarus. These labels should not be treated as a confirmed single identity: the supplied sources do not provide a definitive crosswalk equating UNC4736, Labyrinth Chollima, AppleJeus, Lazarus, and the campaign name Smooth Operator. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [SRC-002](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/) [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

## 1. Initiation and earliest documented compromise

### 1.1 The earlier Trading Technologies compromise

The most specific account of initial access comes from Mandiant. During its investigation of the 3CX incident, Mandiant identified malicious software downloaded from the Trading Technologies website as the initial compromise vector of the 3CX network. It described this as a prior software supply-chain compromise that led to the 3CX software supply-chain compromise. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The relevant malicious artifact was a tampered X_TRADER installer:

- Filename: `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`
- MD5: `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`
- The installer was still available from the legitimate Trading Technologies website in 2022, even though X_TRADER had reportedly been discontinued in 2020.
- The installer and its embedded `Setup.exe` were signed with a certificate associated with Trading Technologies International, Inc.
- The certificate was due to expire in October 2022. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

Execution of `Setup.exe` dropped two malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load one of the malicious DLLs. SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL then decrypted and loaded the payload in memory, ultimately executing VEILEDSIGNAL and two associated modules. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

VEILEDSIGNAL could:

- Send implant data;
- Execute shellcode; and
- Terminate itself.

Its communication component used a named pipe and AES-256-GCM-encrypted communications. The identified sample had MD5 `c6441c961dcad0fe127514a918eaabd4` and used the hard-coded URL:

`www.tradingtechnologies[.]com/trading/order-management`

[SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

### 1.2 Earlier public evidence concerning Trading Technologies

Google Threat Analysis Group reported that `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` was among websites compromised between February 7 and February 9 in its reporting on North Korean Operation AppleJeus activity. That report concerned activity in 2022 and described AppleJeus as North Korean government-backed activity targeting organizations in cryptocurrency, fintech, information technology, and related sectors. [SRC-005](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/)

This provides temporal context for the earlier Trading Technologies compromise, but it does not by itself establish the exact date on which the malicious X_TRADER installer was created, downloaded, or used by a 3CX employee or system. Mandiant’s later forensic reconstruction supplies the connection between the Trading Technologies compromise and the 3CX intrusion. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

### 1.3 What remains uncertain about initial access

The evidence supports the following proposition:

> A malicious X_TRADER installer obtained from the Trading Technologies website was the initial compromise vector into the 3CX network.

That is a Mandiant forensic finding. It is stronger than a general attribution or theory. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

However, the evidence does not establish:

- The precise date when a 3CX user or system downloaded the installer;
- The identity of the affected 3CX user or account;
- Whether the installer was downloaded directly by a person, automatically, or through another system;
- The exact credentials first obtained by the attacker; or
- Whether the Trading Technologies website compromise and the malicious X_TRADER installer were created in one uninterrupted operation.

These points should be reported as unresolved rather than inferred.

### 1.4 Other early observations and why they do not establish a single exact timeline

Several sources reported observations made at different stages of the incident:

- Kaspersky said it opened an investigation into a case involving `guard64.dll` on March 21, approximately one week before the supply-chain attack was discovered. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)
- SentinelOne researchers reportedly observed a spike in behavioral detections beginning March 22. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)
- CrowdStrike observed malicious activity from a legitimately signed 3CX binary, including beaconing and second-stage payload deployment. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)
- Kaspersky stated that CrowdStrike published a report on March 29. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)
- The incident became publicly prominent in late March 2023. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The sources do not reconcile whether these dates represent first compromise, first detection, first deployment of a particular payload, or public disclosure. Therefore, no single precise “first victim” or “first detection” date can be established from the supplied evidence.

## 2. Propagation through the 3CX environment

### 2.1 Lateral movement inside 3CX

Mandiant reported that the attacker used a compiled version of the publicly available Fast Reverse Proxy project to move laterally within the 3CX organization. A file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, was dropped in `C:\Windows\System32`. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

Mandiant reconstructed a sequence in which the attacker:

1. Entered through the malicious Trading Technologies software;
2. Harvested credentials;
3. Moved laterally within the 3CX environment; and
4. Eventually compromised both Windows and macOS build environments. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The supplied evidence does not identify the precise credential, account, workstation, or network path used for each lateral-movement step. The credential-harvesting and lateral-movement sequence is documented at a high level, but the detailed internal chronology remains unavailable.

### 2.2 Compromise of the Windows build environment

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified:

- The TAXHAUL launcher;
- The COLDCAT downloader;
- Persistence through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service; and
- Execution with LocalSystem privileges. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

These findings support the conclusion that the attacker obtained persistent and privileged access to a Windows system involved in 3CX development or release operations. They do not, by themselves, establish which specific build command, signing step, repository, or packaging process was altered.

### 2.3 Compromise of the macOS build environment

Mandiant also determined that the macOS build server was compromised with POOLRAT, using Launch Daemons for persistence. Earlier reporting had identified the sample as SIMPLESEA, but Mandiant’s completed analysis determined that it was POOLRAT rather than a separate malware family. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

Kaspersky separately reported that a macOS 3CX installer had been trojanized. CrowdStrike reported activity on both Windows and macOS, although contemporary reporting noted that other researchers had not yet independently confirmed macOS activity at that time. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

The evidence therefore supports macOS build-environment compromise and macOS package trojanization, while also preserving an early reporting discrepancy about observed macOS activity.

### 2.4 What can be concluded about the build process

The evidence establishes:

- The attacker reached internal 3CX systems;
- Credentials were harvested;
- Lateral movement occurred;
- Both Windows and macOS build environments were compromised;
- Persistence and privileged execution were established on those systems; and
- Tro­janized 3CX releases were subsequently distributed. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The evidence does not establish:

- The exact source-code modification;
- The exact build-pipeline stage altered;
- Whether a source repository, build host, packaging script, signing process, or release server was modified;
- The exact account used to modify the build;
- The exact date of build-environment compromise; or
- Whether the attacker directly altered source code or instead manipulated build infrastructure or release artifacts.

Accordingly, it is accurate to describe the build environment as compromised and the resulting releases as trojanized. It is not accurate, based on the supplied evidence alone, to describe a specific undocumented code-change or pipeline technique as fact.

## 3. Trojanized 3CX DesktopApp releases and payload chain

### 3.1 Affected releases

Mandiant identified 3CX DesktopApp version 18.12.416 and earlier as affected by malicious code. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

Contemporaneous reporting also stated that:

- Huntress had received 2,595 incident reports involving a `3CXDesktopApp.exe` binary that matched known malicious hashes and was signed by 3CX on March 13;
- The Windows Electron application was running update 7; and
- 3CX confirmed that an advanced persistent threat actor was behind a targeted attack. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)

Kaspersky reported that the infection spread through 3CXDesktopApp MSI installers and that a macOS installer was also trojanized. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

The supplied evidence does not provide a complete release-by-release chronology, all affected package hashes, or exact publication dates for every malicious installer.

### 3.2 Mandiant’s payload sequence

Mandiant described malicious code in the affected application that executed SUDDENICON. SUDDENICON obtained additional command-and-control servers from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub. The decrypted command-and-control server was then used to download ICONICSTEALER, which Mandiant described as a dataminer that steals browser information. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The resulting high-level chain was:

1. A signed 3CX application was distributed;
2. The application contained malicious code;
3. SUDDENICON executed;
4. Encrypted GitHub-hosted icon files supplied additional infrastructure;
5. A second-stage server or payload was contacted; and
6. ICONICSTEALER collected browser information. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

### 3.3 Kaspersky’s package and DLL description

Kaspersky described the infection as spreading through infected 3CXDesktopApp MSI installers. The malicious installation package contained an infected DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll` and executed it. The payload extracted command-and-control URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository, connected to one of those servers, downloaded an infostealer, and collected system information and browser history. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

This account overlaps with Mandiant’s description in several important respects:

- Both describe trojanized 3CX software;
- Both describe execution of a malicious component from the application;
- Both describe encrypted or concealed command-and-control information in GitHub-hosted icons; and
- Both describe a later information-stealing payload.

However, the supplied excerpts do not explicitly reconcile the names SUDDENICON and ICONICSTEALER with Kaspersky’s infected DLL, shellcode, and infostealer terminology. They may represent different stages, different samples, or different naming conventions, but that relationship remains unresolved.

### 3.4 Gopuram as a further-stage backdoor

Kaspersky observed `guard64.dll` loaded into an infected `3CXDesktopApp.exe` process and identified it as the main module of the Gopuram backdoor. Gopuram could connect to command-and-control infrastructure, interact with the victim’s file system, create processes, and launch in-memory modules. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

Kaspersky also described other components and persistence mechanisms associated with Gopuram infections, including:

- `wlbsctrl.dll`;
- DLL hijacking through the IKEEXT service;
- Side-loading involving `ualapi.dll` and `ncobjapi.dll`;
- Encrypted shellcode stored under the Windows `TxR` directory;
- Loading into processes such as `spoolsv.exe` and `svchost.exe`; and
- Modules capable of registry, service, file, process-injection, and timestomping operations. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

Kaspersky stated that Gopuram infections increased in March 2023 in direct connection with the 3CX supply-chain attack. It also said that Gopuram was not merely an infostealer, because it provided interactive backdoor functionality. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

## 4. Relationship between the Trading Technologies and 3CX compromises

Mandiant identified technical similarities between the earlier X_TRADER compromise and the 3CX compromise:

- The same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`, was used in SIGFLIP configuration;
- Both used SIGFLIP, a publicly available project associated with CVE-2013-3900;
- Both relied on DAVESHELL, an open-source project for converting PE files into position-independent code or shellcode;
- Both used the cookie variable `__tutma`; and
- Both encrypted data with AES-256-GCM. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

These similarities support Mandiant’s reconstruction that the earlier Trading Technologies compromise led to the 3CX compromise. They also provide technical evidence of common tooling, code reuse, or a related development process.

They do not independently prove that every component was written by the same person or that all activity labels refer to one organization. Publicly available tools and reused code can support attribution, but the supplied sources present the actor identity as an assessment rather than a conclusively demonstrated fact.

## 5. Public attribution

### 5.1 UNC4736

**Status: assessed activity cluster; suspected North Korean nexus; not confirmed as a specific named operator.**

Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736, which it described as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity reported by CISA. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

Mandiant also described varying degrees of overlap between UNC4736 and multiple North Korean operators involved in financially motivated cybercrime, particularly activity focused on cryptocurrency and fintech-related services. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)

The wording “suspected,” “related,” “overlap,” and “moderate confidence” indicates an analytical assessment, not a confirmed public identification of the responsible organization.

### 5.2 Labyrinth Chollima

**Status: CrowdStrike-reported attribution; not independently confirmed by the supplied evidence.**

CrowdStrike associated the attack with Labyrinth Chollima, described as a group linked to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. [SRC-001](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)

The supplied sources do not state whether Labyrinth Chollima is identical to UNC4736, AppleJeus, Lazarus, or another North Korean cluster. The relationship should therefore remain unresolved rather than being merged into a single actor identity.

### 5.3 AppleJeus

**Status: campaign or activity label; relationship to the 3CX operation assessed or inferred.**

Google TAG described Operation AppleJeus as North Korean government-backed activity targeting cryptocurrency and fintech organizations. It reported that `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` was among the compromised websites observed between February 7 and February 9 in the relevant 2022 activity. [SRC-005](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/)

Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky also connected Gopuram with previous AppleJeus activity and shared infrastructure. [SRC-003](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

The evidence does not establish that the entire 3CX operation was officially designated as Operation AppleJeus. It establishes an assessed or inferred relationship.

### 5.4 Lazarus

**Status: indirect or suspected linkage; not confirmed as the actor responsible for the 3CX compromise.**

Kaspersky reported that Gopuram had previously coexisted with AppleJeus in an infection involving a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company. Kaspersky described AppleJeus as a backdoor attributed to the Korean-speaking threat actor Lazarus. [SRC-004](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

This supports a linkage among Gopuram, AppleJeus, and a prior Lazarus attribution. It does not establish that Lazarus conducted the 3CX compromise. Lazarus should therefore be presented as an indirect or suspected attribution, not a confirmed one.

### 5.5 Smooth Operator

**Status: campaign name, not an actor attribution.**

SentinelOne reportedly called the operation “Smooth Operator.” [SRC-002](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)

The available evidence does not identify Smooth Operator as a threat group or organizational identity. It should be retained as a campaign name only.

## 6. Objectives and targeting

Kaspersky reported that some infected systems belonged to cryptocurrency companies and identified fewer than 10 machines ultimately targeted in the cases it observed. It had not observed evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft from those companies. [SRC-002](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)

Kaspersky and WIRED therefore supported the assessment that cryptocurrency organizations were an important target set. SentinelOne researcher Tom Hegel described the theory that attackers initially targeted cryptocurrency firms to enter high-value organizations, but might have developed additional objectives after gaining access to other networks. He also stated that no single security firm could see the full campaign or definitively identify its goals. [SRC-002](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)

The evidence does not establish:

- That cryptocurrency theft was the sole objective;
- That cryptocurrency firms were the only intended victims;
- That cryptocurrency theft actually occurred;
- That all downstream victims were selected for the same reason; or
- That the operation’s objective was exclusively financially motivated.

The safest conclusion is that cryptocurrency and fintech organizations were a documented or assessed target interest, while the broader campaign objective remains unresolved.

## 7. Contradictions and unresolved issues

### 7.1 Timing

The March 21 Kaspersky investigation, March 22 SentinelOne detection spike, CrowdStrike observations, March 29 reporting, and late-March public discovery cannot be combined into a definitive first-access timeline from the supplied sources. These events may represent different detections or stages of an already active intrusion.

### 7.2 Malware terminology

Mandiant used the names SUDDENICON and ICONICSTEALER. Kaspersky described an infected DLL, shellcode extracted from `d3dcompiler_47.dll`, GitHub-hosted icons, and an infostealer. The sources overlap technically but do not explicitly map each malware name to the others.

### 7.3 macOS evidence

CrowdStrike reported activity on macOS, while early reporting said that other researchers had not confirmed it. Kaspersky reported that a macOS installer was trojanized, and Mandiant documented compromise of the macOS build server. The evidence supports macOS involvement but preserves uncertainty about the timing and scope of observed macOS victim activity.

### 7.4 Actor names

Labyrinth Chollima, UNC4736, AppleJeus, Lazarus, and Smooth Operator are different source-specific labels. The available evidence does not prove that they all refer to the same actor or operation. They should not be collapsed into a single confirmed entity.

### 7.5 3CX’s internal postmortem

3CX confirmed that an advanced persistent threat actor was behind a targeted attack affecting its Windows Electron application and said that it planned a later analysis. The supplied benchmark evidence does not include that later 3CX analysis. No additional internal 3CX conclusions should be inferred.

## Conclusion

The public evidence chain supported by the supplied sources is:

1. Trading Technologies infrastructure or software was compromised.
2. A malicious X_TRADER installer remained available from the legitimate Trading Technologies website.
3. A 3CX system obtained and executed that malicious software.
4. VEILEDSIGNAL and associated components enabled further access.
5. The attacker harvested credentials and moved laterally within 3CX.
6. Windows and macOS build environments were compromised.
7. Persistent malware was installed on those build systems.
8. Tro­janized 3CX DesktopApp packages were produced and distributed.
9. The packages executed downloaders and information-stealing payloads, with Gopuram deployed in some cases.
10. Public attribution focused on a suspected North Korean nexus, with source-specific links to UNC4736, Labyrinth Chollima, AppleJeus, and indirectly Lazarus.
11. No supplied source conclusively establishes a single confirmed actor identity or fully resolves the exact initial-access and build-pipeline chronology.

Where the evidence does not establish a point, it should be reported as unresolved rather than omitted if it is material to the reconstruction.
